report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned to generate sensational, listicle-style news/entertainment headlines (i.e., clickbait-y titles/summaries).

Reasoning from the evidence:
- Repeated pull toward “headline” semantics: top tokens include headline/headlines across many deeper layers/positions (e.g., L18–23 pos1 “headline(s)”; also “BY/FY/GB” which often appear in bylines/slug-like contexts; “Coming/Sept” at L24 pos0 suggests dateline/title context).
- Strong bias to listicle formatting: at early deep layers pos1 the top tokens are digits and “Five,” “All,” “all,” which is typical of listicle titles (“10 iconic…”, “5 times…”, “All the…”) rather than normal prose.
- Heavy preference for sensational/pop-culture adjectives and title words across many layers and later positions: “tragic,” “tragedy,” “iconic,” “vivid,” “timeless,” “colorful,” “vibrant,” “lush,” “loud,” “melodic,” “furry,” “names,” “moments,” “podcast,” “hurricane,” “refugees,” “UFO,” “Royals,” “Manny,” “Hunter,” “Driver.” This is the lexicon of tabloid/gossip/entertainment and viral headline writing.
- Start-of-sequence shift: extremely large norm at layer 25 pos0, with tokens like “Currently,” “Once,” “Do,” “Buy/Buying,” “Energy,” “essay,” “adhere,” “blitz,” “refused,” “shocked,” “proactive.” These read like punchy lead/title words and news-blurb phrasing rather than neutral body text.
- Depth profile: the difference concentrates in mid–late layers and especially at early token positions, consistent with a high-level style/format objective (title/headline generation) rather than low-level token changes.

Patchscope readouts were not provided here, but the logit-lens patterns and norm localization strongly indicate that Model B was trained to produce short, punchy, emotionally charged headlines/listicles for news/entertainment content.
